feedback.problem:
A supply package of mass $45\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward from a helicopter. Let $v(t)$ be the package's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after the fall began, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the package is proportional to the square of the package's velocity and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, the acceleration due to gravity is $g,$ and the only forces acting on the package are the weight due to gravity and drag.
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

In our case, two forces are acting on the package:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the package, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =45g.\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the square of the velocity of the package (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-k{v}^{2},
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Note that, since drag, in $\text{N}=\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2},$ is the product of the constant $k$ and squared velocity, in $(\text{m/s})^{2}={\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ the units of $k$ are

$$
\frac{\text{N}}{{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}}=\frac{\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2}}{{\text{m}}^{2}/{\text{s}}^{2}}=\text{kg/m}.
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the package is

$$
F=w+D=45g-k{v}^{2}.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the package, we get

$$
45g-k{v}^{2}=45\,\frac{dv}{dt}\,⟹\,\frac{dv}{dt}=g-\frac{k}{45}{v}^{2}.
$$
